title: Her father ran the line for 40 years. As his successor, she shut it down
name: Mariko Hayase
text: Three years after she took over, orders for their main product — auto parts — had halved. What remained: craftsmen who’d worked for her father, and a production line losing money. She shut down her father’s main production line. Orders for their core auto parts fell by half in three years. She shut the mass-production line and focused on prototype machining. No craftsman left, and revenue recovered within two years.

title: He started the company with his best friend from college. Then he asked him to leave
name: Takuma Nakamura
text: Two founders, equal titles, equal shares. By the time they had 30 employees, nobody could make the final call. He asked his co-founder to step down. With equal shares and equal authority, nobody had the final say. After six months of talks, he asked his co-founder to step down. They still go out for a drink together once a year.

title: He left to protect it: 143 days to walk away from the company he founded
name: Keisuke Mori
text: He believed nothing would move without him — until he admitted that he was the one holding the company back. He walked away from the company he built. Every decision ran through the founder, and the organization slowed down. Before choosing a successor, he gave up his own role. Over 143 days he handed over authority and stepped outside.

title: She knew it would fail. It still took her a year to stop
name: Nao Kuroda
text: The losses grew every month, and so did the messages from customers who believed in the product. Every signal said stop. She rewrote her own exit criteria three times. She made herself keep her own exit rule. Revenue was growing, but few customers stayed past three months. Encouraging messages led her to move the exit line three times. She made the rule impossible to change alone — and closed the business.

title: The morning after he decided to close the company, he couldn’t say a word
name: Ryo Saeki
text: Revenue had fallen by two-thirds, and the cash would last two more months. He came in to announce the shutdown — and found his team had spent the night writing a rescue plan. He put the shutdown on hold. Once. Two months of cash left, and the CEO had decided to close. Faced with a rescue plan his team wrote overnight, he held back the announcement. He chose to keep the customers, not the size of the company.
